title: Millions of Workers Shut Down Spain With First General Strike in 14 Years
content:
Spanish workers braved stormy weather to go on general strike in protest against the country’s housing crisis on Wednesday.




Unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers, as millions downed tools three weeks before a snap general election. There were 

“total stoppages”

 at Volkswagen’s factory in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona, organisers said.




Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector are also taking part, they added. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% are striking while 35% of postal service workers have also joined.




The 24-hour strike, Spain’s first in 14 years, is backed by the country’s two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants’ associations fighting rising rents and evictions.




“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.




Mass protest marches were planned for Wednesday afternoon despite the expected arrival of two storms, Charles and Bruna.




Unions pointed to a 10% drop in electricity demand across the country, saying it shows that activity in energy-intensive industries such as steel processing had come to a halt.




Barcelona’s metro is only running during peak commuting hours

The incident had a “profound effect on her mental health and her wellbeing,” he said.




It had been a “struggle” for her to “see him in the media, still getting jobs, still being able to conduct himself in public life.”




McNamara said: “I reported it to authorities and broadcasters.”




Asked if any action was taken, he said, “Not that I’m aware of, no… He was still on TV for many, many years. He was still allowed to, by the sounds of it, be involved with other young women – no.”




Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

title: US Firm Linked to Gaza Aid Site Massacres to Help With Burnham’s 10-Year Plan
content:
Andy Burnham’s government has hired a US consultancy firm that helped set up a group to run “aid” sites in Gaza where Israeli forces massacred starving civilians. 




Boston Consulting Group (BCG) will advise on Burnham’s his 10-year plan, the Times reported. The plan, which has yet to be published, has been billed as part of the prime minister’s pledge to end decades of neoliberalism in the UK. 




BCG last year had to 

publicly disavow its role

 in creating the notorious Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), which operated four sites where

 

hundreds

 of people were killed

 while trying to get food in 2025, as Israel deliberately starved Gaza’s population.  




BCG, one of the ‘big three’ global consulting firms, was also involved last year in Donald Trump’s plan to turn Gaza into a riviera, which would effectively amount to ethnic cleansing. As part of those plans, it produced a financial model for a scenario where Palestinians were ethnically cleansed from Gaza. 




It built the model two months after Trump suggested emptying Gaza of its inhabitants, 

the Financial Times reported

.




“Aside from an obvious point that you don’t appoint companies like the Boston Consulting Group if you have any actual intention of ending 40 years of neoliberalism, Trump’s ‘Gaza Riviera’ blueprint is clear ethnic cleansing,” Green party leader Zack Polanski said in a statement.

Investigate Europe has revealed.




One electrical tester was left with electrical burns on 12% of his body after performing an overtime task without safety equipment at a Google data centre site in Belgium. His burns are still so severe he can barely stand being touched, 

he told reporters

. No fines or sanctions are known to have been issued.




At a Microsoft development in Sweden, Romanian workers employed by a subcontractor described overcrowded accommodation infested with rats, broken ventilation and poor heating. 




One diabetic worker had his toe amputated after his feet reportedly lost circulation in the inadequate work boots issued by the contractor, while others contracted tuberculosis.

content:

Having watched their tax dollars flow in unchecked torrents to Israel, an illegal war in Iran and corporate welfare programmes, American workers, burdened by high fuel, food and healthcare costs, finally said ‘enough’. 




The ball is now in the Democrats’ court, with the party controlling both the Senate and the House of Representatives from January. But what’s their game plan? Big Thumps – taking aim at risky but headline grabbing knock-outs? Or Top Trumps – smaller, frequent battles for safer wins? 




And can they even play as a team at all?







If there’s one thing that Democrats historically excel at, it’s misreading the public mood. We saw that in 2024, when presidential candidate Kamala Harris failed to harness public anger over Gaza while offering little to allay growing economic distress. She was rightly punished for it. 




Misunderstanding their new position is the most fatal error Democrats could make at this juncture. It must be tempting, high on a win, to see the blue wave as a love bomb from the nation. But when you win big because a 

national majority loathes the president

Now China’s researchers make world-class cancer drugs, cheap surgical robots and cutting edge brain-computer interfaces. Its doctors make AI-powered avatars of themselves to deal with ever more patients.




But China is growing old before it grows rich. Cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer’s and cardiovascular problems are ballooning. And its aging crisis is coming on faster because of the legacy of its one-child policy. How will China adapt?




Ruby Wang worked on the NHS Covid frontline before becoming Head of Health at the British Embassy in Beijing. And now she’s written 

The China Cure: The Rise of Biotech, AI Medicine and a Global Health Superpower

. She tells Richard Hames how China got from barefoot doctors to high-tech hospitals, what it learned from Covid, and what the NHS could learn from China.

content:
With eyes on politics internationally, it’s hard not to feel hope-pilled this week after Donald Trump and the Republican party received a historic battering in the US midterms.




The president told voters to

 

pretend he was on the ballot

. They used the opportunity to raise a middle finger to him, Elon Musk – who

AI data centres

.




The

 

midterms’ “bluenami”

, along with Lula’s stunning win in Brazil and the

 

student-led movement

 that defeated Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić, represent a wave of progressive victories globally. So why does the landscape at home feel so… grey?

With Andy Burnham now beyond his first 100 days in power, the view from his premiership is looking rather overcast. On Thursday,

 

Burnham told the Economist

in his first speech as PM

 back in July? – may be delayed into 2027.




Sure, maybe Old Eyelashes is taking his time dotting all the ‘i’s and crossing every ‘t’, but sources were briefing that last week’s milquetoast budget was low-key

 

precisely because

 big things were being held back for the ten-year plan.




And frankly, the budget hasn’t had nearly enough hate for being embarrassingly unambitious at a time when people who actually want to live here (not the high-net-worth individuals who are always just about to flee over the mere hint of wealth taxes) are crying out for actual change.




The budget’s £100 sticking-plaster

 

energy bung for households

 in four council tax bands does nothing to solve the long-term cost-of-living crisis or improve British energy security. And this seems to be something of a pattern – big talk and puny delivery. Take the failed monopoly on water: the

 

eight new regional water councils

 announced yesterday will allow local leaders to “set priorities” and “shape billions of pounds of investment” but, crucially, they do not put water back into public ownership.




This is to say nothing of the climate-illiterate decision to green-light new gas drilling in the North Sea, and murmurs that approval of the much more damaging new Rosebank oil field was

 

baked into the budget

.




Alongside the can-kicking and edge-tinkering, there’s also Burnham’s admission in the summer that his government

 

“got it wrong” on Gaza

 and foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s appeal at Labour conference to everyone horrified by the slaughter of Palestinians:

 

“You were right.”

 Both statements are ageing like a tuna sandwich stuffed behind a radiator (if you can afford to turn yours on, of course).




Burnham has

 

rejected Jeremy Corbyn’s call

 for a Chilcot-style public inquiry into Britain’s role in Israel’s genocide, which means the UK public continues to be kept in the dark about the military, economic and diplomatic assistance rendered to a rogue state, in our names and with our tax money, over the past three years.




What’s more, the government has been defending its Starmer-era proscription of direct action group Palestine Action in the supreme court this week, while grannies, the children of Holocaust survivors and a CBE were arrested outside under the Terrorism Act. Why? Because they

 

held paper signs quoting the wife of the PM’s national security adviser

.




And peaceful protesters opposing the ban on Palestine Action have reportedly been handed bail conditions barring them from any protest in support of… Palestine. Not Palestine Action –

 

Palestine in general

. Burnham’s willingness to keep this authoritarian and antidemocratic farce going is damning, and the footage of retirees being carried away by cops makes Britain a laughing stock on the global stage.




When we can see so much hope elsewhere – from communities united across party lines

 

against sprawling, energy-hungry data centres

 and the anti-human technology they serve, to

 

Brazil’s digital mass mobilisation strategy

 becoming a beacon of global leftist inspiration – the landscape at home can feel frustratingly dreary.




Blame my chronic low dopamine or the leaden November sky for this doomerism, but without strong opposition from Labour’s left, this government will be content to sink back into the centrist torpor of the Starmer years. And we all know how that story plays out – with an emboldened far right and a country run in service of corporate elites, at the expense of everyone else.

title: Google UK Signs ‘Sweetheart Deal’ With Employer-Friendly Union
content:
Google UK has been accused of signing a “sweetheart deal” with an employer-friendly union to undermine workers’ ability to organise within the tech company. 




Google 

signed an access agreement with Prospect union on Monday

 to make inroads among its 7,000 UK workers – excluding DeepMind staff – after 

new rights for unions to access workplaces

 in Britain came into force last week.




However, critics say Prospect lacks a strong record of organising with Google employees – known as Googlers – in the UK. The two largest and most active unions in Google UK are Unite and the Communication Workers’ Union (CWU) via their United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) branch. 




Prospect was granted access to the Google UK workforce over Unite and the CWU, despite the latter two unions applying for access as soon as formally possible. This means Prospect can now 

communicate with non-unionised workers

 and encourage them to join. 




In a joint Unite and CWU statement to members seen by Novara Media, the two unions warned that Prospect’s agreement with Google is only for “occasional meetings and an internal page, falling far short of the legal minimum requested by your unions”. 




A Google UK software engineer and UTAW rep, speaking to Novara Media on the condition of anonymity due to fear of professional reprisals, called the deal “a huge slap in the face for me and all UTAW and Unite organisers in Google”.  




The software engineer said: “We have worked diligently over the past few years to represent our fellow Googlers’ needs through collective action. We fought to keep as many jobs as possible during redundancies, we demonstrated against Google’s military contracts, and we demanded a stronger, worker-led regulation on Google and DeepMind’s AI direction. 




“For all of our fastidious work, our request for a right as basic as access has been ignored and given to Prospect, a union with laughably low membership in Google which has not participated in a single one of our aforementioned struggles.”




Unite and the CWU are asking why Prospect, which has not engaged in member-led unionising activity at Google, was granted access so quickly and alleging that the Prospect deal was pre-planned because Prospect may be considered a “tamer” or more employer-friendly union.




The Google software engineer added: “This conduct by Google is an insidious way to undermine worker organisation while veiling themselves in the guise of a benevolent, pro-union company. It is telling that this deal was conducted by Google UK’s current senior labour relations consultant, Philip Bickerstaffe, an ex-national officer at Prospect.”




Bickerstaffe worked at Prospect as a national officer from 2004 to 2011, according to his LinkedIn profile, before going on to roles with BT, Boeing, Amazon and Google. 




The Prospect-Google deal follows 

a similar agreement

 between Prospect and Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and Whatsapp. Meta employs roughly 5,000 people in the UK. 




Right of access to workplaces in the UK – even where employers are hostile to trade unions organising onsite – was included in the Employment Rights Act 2025, and came into force on 30 October. 




Unite and the CWU say they put in an access request at the stroke of midnight on 30 October, and received a formal acknowledgement from Google on 3 November, which said their request would be considered and responded to “within the appropriate time frame”.




Employers then have 15 days to respond and a further 25 days to negotiate. The Prospect deal was announced on 2 November, suggesting that little, if any, time was spent negotiating the terms of the deal, which has added to the impression that the deal is favourable to the employer.




Unite, the CWU and Prospect are all members of the Trade Union Congress (TUC), which means they must 

respect the principle

 that a union shouldn’t organise at a workplace where another union already has the majority of workers as members or is actively engaged in significant organising activity. 




Unite and the CWU say Prospect has violated this national cross-union agreement by signing the access deal with Google UK. 




A Prospect spokesperson said: “These allegations are false and seem designed to undermine union organising at Google. Our access agreement with Google was agreed in accordance with the TUC principles and does not include Google DeepMind where other unions are making a recognition bid.” 




A spokesperson from Google UK said: “To comply with new UK workplace legislation, we have established a structured access agreement with Prospect union for Google’s UK employees, but not including Google DeepMind. This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfill these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on.” 




Unite and the CWU have assured members that they are escalating the matter through the appropriate channels.

title: Palestine Action Protesters Arrested for Quoting Wife of Prime Minister’s Advisor
content:
Twenty-five peaceful protesters were arrested under terror legislation outside the supreme court in London on Wednesday, as the controversial ban on Palestine Action undergoes its final legal challenge on British soil. 




Retirees, health workers, the children of Holocaust survivors, a CBE and a professor held signs quoting the writer Sarah Helm, who posted on X last month, “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” . They swapped the word “authors” for their own descriptor, such as “Jews”, “physiotherapists”, “son of a Holocaust survivor”, “gardeners” or 

“normal people”

. 




Everybody who held these signs was arrested on suspicion of supporting a proscribed terrorist organisation under section 13 of the Terrorism Act. 




Helm is married to the prime minister’s national security advisor, Jonathan Powell. The Metropolitan police 

chose not to take action over her post 

, saying it “did not meet the criminal threshold”.




Many of those outside the court decried this apparent “double standard” in the enforcement of the Palestine Action ban. Officers seemed initially confused about what they should do. Novara Media heard some debating the meaning of the protesters’ placards and whether or not they should make arrests. 




The majority of those protesting outside the supreme court were over the age of 50, as has been the case at all demos against the ban organised by Defend Our Juries (DOJ) over the 15 months of the proscription being in force. 




Actor Alfie Enoch and Massive Attack frontman Robert Del Naja were outside court in support of the protesters. Enoch, who played Dean Thomas in seven Harry Potter films, told Novara Media that the arrests of peaceful protesters happening around him were “chilling and frightening”. He held a sign reading: “This is democracy, not terrorism.” 




Del Naja said he hopes “common sense prevails” at the supreme court, telling Novara Media: “Direct action is not terrorism. These are people acting on conscience to prevent lethal drones destined for the civilian population of Gaza – that to me is a patriotic duty.” 




Among those arrested were Jonathon Porritt CBE, a former advisor to the government, and academic Peter Hallward. Professor Hallward organised a letter delivered to the president of the supreme court, which was signed by 150 leading professors – including dozens of UK law professors – and 1,500 members of the public. It read: “We oppose genocide so we support Palestine Action.”




Porritt, a professor with the Centre for Research in Modern European Philosophy, told Novara Media that preventing genocide is an “absolutely moral obligation and legal duty” and compared defying the ban on Palestine Action to the historic actions of the suffragettes and the abolitionists. 




Trudi Warner, a 71-year-old retired social worker and DOJ co-founder, told Novara Media, that the ban is a “complete mess” and “we’ve managed to show what a mess it is”. “It’s cost the police and the taxpayer millions of pounds to enforce a law that’s obviously ridiculous – it has to stop.”




Warner was arrested for holding a sign that read, “God help us artists who support Palestine and Palestine Action” as she enjoys art in her retirement. 




Tom Southerden, Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director, called the arrests “appalling” and said that people being arrested for using the same language as Sarah Helm “shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are”.




A DOJ spokesperson said: “Now we understand what the Met meant when they said Sarah Helm’s message ‘did not meet the criminal threshold’. If you say you support Palestine Action and you’re married to the national security advisor that doesn’t meet the criminal threshold. But if you’re not married to the national security advisor it does.




“Let’s hope the supreme court takes into account the blatantly discriminatory application of this crazy law.”




A Met spokesperson said: “

Officers have arrested a total of 25 people outside the Supreme Court on suspicion of expressing support for a proscribed organisation. The policing operation is ongoing and officers will continue to arrest those who break the law.”




Why is Palestine Action in court?




Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori is challenging whether the UK government’s decision to proscribe the direct action group as a terrorist organisation last summer was lawful. 




It’s Ammori’s last chance to appeal in the UK, and she was granted permission to do so on one ground: whether the proscription of Palestine Action is compatible with Articles 10 (the right to free expression) and 11 (the right to freedom of peaceful assembly) of the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR). 




Ammori has confirmed that if her appeal to the supreme court is unsuccessful, she will take her case to the European Court of Human Rights.




Justices will hear arguments over two days (4 and 5 November). This includes interventions in support of Ammori’s case from writers’ associations PEN International and English PEN, Amnesty International UK and Liberty, a UK Jewish Bloc, and UN special rapporteur Ben Saul. 




The Jewish Bloc, made up of 11 Jewish and Jewish-led groups, seeks to challenge the “fundamental fallacy” that Palestine Action targeted or otherwise posed a threat to the Jewish community, or that it was in any way motivated by antisemitism. It also highlights the particular impact of the proscription of on the Article 10 and Article 11 ECHR rights of the pro-Palestinian Jewish community.




Ammori first took the UK government to court 

in November 2025

, marking the first time a banned group has been able to legally challenge its proscription via judicial review in British history. The high court 

decided in February this year

 that the decision to ban Palestine Action was unlawful because it was incompatible with articles 10 and 11 of the ECHR and that then-home secretary Yvette Cooper breached her own policy in the proscription process. 




The government appealed the high court’s decision, and the court of appeal – the next court up the chain – sided with the government, 

ruling the ban on Palestine Action lawful

 in June.




Since Palestine Action was proscribed, approximately 4,000 people protesting the ban have been arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000, causing 

a record-breaking spike

 in terror-related arrests.

title: Met Police Hire Bus to Help With Mass Arrest of Elderly People Holding Signs
content:
Police hired a private bus to help cart away scores of peaceful protesters defying the ban on Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Saturday. 




Around 400 people – many of them elderly – held signs expressing support for the proscribed group at the rally, which aimed to draw attention to Donald Trump’s alleged role in the ban.




Despite bringing dozens of police vans to the protest, officers also used a privately hired vehicle from Kent-based bus operator GoBus to transport arrestees.




“There were so many people defying the ban they had to bring in a bus to take more people to the police station – something we’ve never seen before,” a spokesperson for protest organisers Defend Our Juries (DOJ) said. 




Some protesters sang the nursery rhyme the Wheels on the Bus as police carried people into the vehicle.




The Metropolitan police 

said Saturday evening

 that at least 139 people had been arrested and arrests were still ongoing. 




The DOJ spokesperson said that, as a result of Saturday’s demonstration, the total number of people arrested for supporting Palestine Action since July 2025 

has exceeded 4,000

.




One woman was arrested Saturday for holding a placard repeating the words of writer Sarah Helm, the wife of national security advisor Jonathan Powell. Helm wrote, “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” in a post on X on 15 October. 




Two days later, the Met said the post “did not meet the criminal threshold” – and yet on Saturday its officers arrested a protester for using the same phrase, except that the word “authors” had been substituted for “retirees”.    




Police made no arrests at a simultaneous protest outside the US consulate in Edinburgh.




The DOJ spokesperson said these inconsistencies in the policing of the two protests made a “mockery” of the ban: “You can be arrested for defying it in England but not Scotland.” 




“How can Andy Burnham possibly justify arrests today for holding up words which, just weeks ago, were deemed to be below the criminal threshold when expressed by the wife of his own national security advisor?” the group added in a statement. “This makes a further mockery of the proscription, which becomes more impossible to sustain by the day.”




Activists at both protests said Trump had played a role in the proscription of Palestine Action in the UK. The US president is suspected of pressuring then prime minister Keir Starmer to ban the group after its activists painted the words “Gaza is not 4 sale” on the lawn of his golf course in Turnberry, Scotland in March last year.




“The government was wrong to equate throwing paint on a golf course with dropping bombs,” retired financial advisor Marji Mansfield, 78, told Novara Media. “It’s Halloween and this is a complete horror story – what Trump wants is dictating policy in the UK.”




In a March Truth Social post, Trump claimed prime minister Keir Starmer had informed him the UK “caught the terrorists who attacked the beautiful Turnberry”. 




“That’s why all this is happening – because the mad emperor is upset because his golf course has been sprayed,” Tim Crosland, a former government lawyer and DOJ co-founder, told Novara Media. 




Ahead of Saturday’s demonstration, police had 

threatened to arrest

 not just people expressing support for Palestine Action but anyone providing them with “logistical support”.  




Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has argued that the ban on Palestine Action followed democratic process and was “

endorsed by Parliament

”. That claim is weakened by allegations of a foreign president’s involvement, Crosland said. 




An appeal to overturn the ban is due to begin on 4 November at the Supreme Court. 




This August, Trump imposed sanctions on Palestine Action in the US, with the Department of the Treasury labelling it a “transnational terrorist group”. 




As a result, the group’s co-founder 

Huda Ammori was blocked

 from raising funds to challenge the group’s proscription. 




“As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist is beyond hypocritical,” Ammori said at the time. 




Retired professor Tony Booth, 81, said the ban was “the wildest piece of legislation I’ve ever seen in my lifetime”. Recalling his five previous arrests for supporting the group, the pensioner said officers often seemed “a bit apologetic”.




“They’re arresting some old bloke, they know I’m not a terrorist,” he said. 




Since October 2023, the US has sent 

at least $25.5bn worth of military assistance

 to Israel.

title: I’m a Teacher. The Bell Antisemitism Report Will Silence My Pro-Palestine Pupils
content:
If you’ve seen the news in the past week or so, you’d be forgiven for believing that antisemitism is the single most pressing issue facing British education today. All schools in England have been told they must consider antisemitism a distinct form of harm after recommendations from 

a review

 by former Ofsted chief Sir David Bell were 

accepted by the government 

last week. 




As a secondary school teacher of ten years, I can’t help but feel like we aren’t being told the full story here. Bell is hardly an impartial figure, given his membership of a pro-Israel, anti-BDS 

academic charity

 and the 

anti-Muslim comments

 he made during his tenure as Ofsted head. Then there’s the report’s widely-shared finding that “almost three in five” Jewish pupils have experienced antisemitism at school. This would be a sobering statistic about any minority group, but it 

just doesn’t stand up to scrutiny

. The report even admits that the “low sample size of 92 students who identify as Jewish should be treated with caution”.




The Bell review uses the controversial 

International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) 

definition of antisemitism – which states that calling the state of Israel a racist endeavour or comparing Israel’s actions to that of the Nazis constitutes anti-Jewish hate – and calls on schools to adopt it. In other words, anti-Zionism equals antisemitism. A 

2025 survey

 found that 45% of British adults agreed with the statement “Israel treats the Palestinians like the Nazis treated the Jews”, so by this definition, almost half the British population are raging antisemites. Amongst young people, the figure was as high as 60%. 




Now, I teach in a very Muslim borough of east London and my pupils are, to put it mildly, extremely passionate about the Palestinian cause. They attend rallies with their parents on the weekend, wear pin badges on their backpacks and have watched a campaign of genocide against children like themselves livestreamed through their phones for the past three years. 




I have never witnessed any genuinely anti-Jewish statements, and I’m not alone in that experience amongst colleagues. Schools are not the cesspits of antisemitic hate that the media and government would have us believe, and young people are far more capable of nuanced debate than they are given credit for. But none of that seems to matter, because under the IHRA definition, criticism of Israel or rejection of Zionism is enough to constitute antisemitism – and therein lies the problem. Is this about supporting Jewish children or is it about silencing support for Palestine altogether?




The most troubling thing about the Bell review is that it masquerades as concern for Jewish pupils and teachers whilst actually functioning as a continuation of the government’s 

ongoing clampdown

 on pro-Palestine expression in all areas of public life. The 

report seems more concerned with banning Palestine badges and ensuring teachers are ‘politically impartial’ when it comes to the state of Israel than it does about what sort of support should be extended to victims of anti-Jewish discrimination. 




The idea that teachers should be trained specifically on antisemitism, as a form of hate entirely distinct from all other types of bigotry, speaks to a hierarchy of discrimination in the UK. Some forms of prejudice are embedded in the very system itself – consider the Prevent duty placed upon all teachers that 

disproportionately impacts Muslim children

 – while others get immediate government attention and resourcing. 




My fear is that the Bell recommendations will pressure schools into cracking down on pro-Palestine expression at the cost of tackling genuine racism – and that’s before you consider the impact on underpaid and overstretched teachers having yet another priority to add to their overflowing lists when there are still young people to support and lessons to teach. 




Free speech and equality for all will likely go out the window in favour of blanket bans on all discussions of Palestine in the classroom – and undoubtedly this will have a disproportionate impact on Muslim pupils and staff. Given that Prevent referrals for wearing pro-Palestine items have 

risen in recent years

, those already facing heightened suspicion and even criminalisation are likely to be further targeted.




It feels particularly sinister that this move to essentially outlaw criticism of Israel and solidarity with Palestinians – from condemning the Israeli state to wearing a flag pin – should be inflicted upon schools of all places. What happened to the notion that our educational institutions should be alive with debate and critical thinking, free speech and nuance? What are we teaching the next generation if condemning a genocide in their classroom equates to racial hatred? 




The answer, soberingly, seems to be that this is the very point. A British state 

complicit in the genocide of Palestinians

 has no interest in a generation of politically-engaged children who will one day hold it to account. Less about protecting Jewish pupils and staff, this report is more about manufacturing consent for Israel’s crimes and Britain’s long, bloody history of propping it up. 

If teachers are scared into silence and children are taught that it is offensive to question a live genocide, schools become factories training tomorrow’s adults to never question the status quo. How convenient for the state.

title: The Mao Era – Catastrophe or Necessity?
content:
No one is disputed like Mao. Was he a mass murderer, a Communist hero, a charlatan, or a great poet? The saviour of the peasants, or the man who extracted from them all that he could?




Mao’s biography is a nest of contradictions. He led the largest revolution in world history, then presided over its largest famine – and even then, life expectancy rose 20 years over the course of his rule. He launched rebellions – against a government he already controlled. He purged his enemies and friends alike.




Some 50 years after his death, he remains a central figure in Chinese politics. The Communist Party of China posthumously declared him to be 70% right and 30% wrong, but his face still hangs over Tiananmen Square.

In one placard, a hand drawn Homer Simpson told President Macron that disturbances in 2019 and 2023 were just the worst protests of his life “so far”, indicating that the movement does not intend to lie down easily.




Students have been on the march or blockading their schools since 17 September, but this time they were joined by trade unionists and yellow vest protesters supporting student demands, protesting against the rising cost of living and rejecting the upcoming austerity budget. The convergence of different movements that have erupted under the Macron presidency could be heard in the songs and chants of the crowd. There was “on est la” (“we are here”) the defiant song of the “yellow vest” movement, chants of free Palestine, as well as adapted versions of songs against Macron’s pension reform which were recycled to apply to education.

title: China’s Century of Revolutions
content:
For a century, China underwent a series of invasions, revolutions and counter-revolutions. In China, it’s known as the Century of Humiliation.




It was a time of immense upheavals: from the Opium Wars of 1839, through the Taiping Rebellion, the Xinhai Republican Revolution, a Civil War, an invasion by the Japanese which merged into the Second World War; the resumption of the Civil War and, eventually coming to an end with the Communist Revolution of 1949.




Each one transformed the country more comprehensively than seemed possible beforehand.




Rebecca Karl is the author of 

China’s Revolutions in the Modern World

, which tells us not only what happened, but how its participants tried to make sense of it all, and why that still matters for understanding China now – after all, the Chinese Communist Party haven’t forgotten any of it.




She joined Richard Hames to discuss the century that destroyed imperial China and set the stage for the largest revolution in history.

title: More US Soldiers Have Died in Iran War Than Pentagon Previously Admitted
content:
The Pentagon has quietly revealed that more US troops have been killed and wounded in the Iran war than it 

previously admitted

. 




Twenty-one service members have been killed during the conflict and 865 wounded, according to data released without an announcement last Friday on an 

official US military website

. 




A previous data release in August showed 18 killed and 757 wounded, while another last month listed 18 deaths and 820 wounded. 




As fighting has lulled for many weeks, it seems unlikely that the casualties are the result of fresh combat. The Intercept, which has been investigating undercounted casualties in the war for months, reported that one of the newly acknowledged deaths was on 6 March. 




An anonymous defence official told the outlet earlier this year that the US military was engaging in a “casualty cover-up”.




The latest change to the tally was made after 

US politicians highlighted

 “a discrepancy in the Pentagon’s reporting of casualty numbers”.




US war secretary Pete Hegseth has furiously denounced journalists who previously reported that casualties from the war are higher than the military admits. In response to a 

Washington Post story

 last month, he 

posted

: “This is DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE.”

title: Lula Accuses Meta of Interfering in Brazil’s Election by Restricting His Posts
content:
​Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has accused Meta of interfering in the country’s election by restricting his activity on its platforms.




​The social media giant “prevented president Lula’s profile from promoting Instagram feed posts,” his 

campaign said

, adding that a post from his official account “experienced an interruption in view counts, which affected its reach.”




The accusation comes after Lula’s campaign found it was

 

temporarily unable

 to post Facebook ads in September, while far-right election disinformation appeared to circulate widely. 




Amnesty International research found last month that Meta

 

failed to stop ads

 featuring false claims about where to vote and calling for the military to “take back power”.




​Lula came second behind far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in a first round of voting on 4 October, and the race now goes to a run-off on 25 October that Bolsonaro is considered more likely to win.




Lula’s campaign said that before the 4 October vote, his profile “suddenly disappeared from Instagram’s search function” along with those of other leftwing leaders.
